newsitem.title: FRANCE: Domestic support shelters French bonds from storm.
newsitem.headline: Domestic support shelters French bonds from storm.

text.p: While fears of U.S. monetary tightening rattle European bond investors, the French market looks well protected because of the small percentage of domestic debt in outside hands, independent economists say.

France would not escape unscathed from a big shakeout in the U.S. debt market. But "we expect it to fall relatively less than other European markets -- essentially because foreign ownership of domestic debt is so low," Marie Owens-Thomsen of Banque International du Placement said.
Most recent official figures for December 1996 showed just 12 percent of outstanding French government notes and bonds in foreign hands. That compared with nearly 40 percent in 1994.
"That, in itself, insulates France from any big speculative flows in capital," Owens-Thomsen said. Non-resident investors in Germany, by contrast, hold 38 percent of the market.
"German debt is much more exposed and is, in that sense, one of the riskiest European markets," another economist said.
Also supporting the French market is a massive reallocation of savings under way since last year as investors shift out of money market funds in response to falling interest rates.

This move is believed to have injected to 16 billion to 20 billion francs ($2.8 billion to $3.5 billion) into the bond market in the first quarter and around 7.5 billion francs into equities. "Our forecast for the year as a whole is that 80 to 100 billion francs will move into the bond market," Owens-Thomsen said. "That's about a fifth of the issuance programme of the French treasury."

During 1996, about 450 billion to 500 billion francs were believed to have flowed from money market funds and tax free "Livret A" savings plans into longer term savings such as life insurance contracts which are mostly invested in bonds.

To this bond friendly environment, analysts say, can be added low interest rates, slow growth, high unemployment, a firm currency and weak inflation. Inflation rose just 0.1 percent in March from February and was up 1.1 percent on the year.

These events are reflected in the yields of French 10-year bonds or Obligations Assimilables du Tresor (OATs) over their German counterparts. In 1990, 10-year OATs yielded two percentage points more than Bunds but the gap has closed and French yields are lower. Bunds were yielding 13 basis more than OATs on Monday and analysts said that gap could widen to 18.
"These foreign holdings in the market are so small that France, by default, is outperforming Germany in a falling market," Phyllis Reed of BZW said.
Still, analysts say the French market may be close to peaking, especially with European monetary union, which should bring yields in France and Germany to parity when it starts in 1999.
"If we really believe in monetary union, investors will look at Bunds as cheap OATs," Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais said. He added that the French market could be vulnerable to "some correction."
At the same time, though, analysts say restrictions barring life insurers from putting more than 20 percent of their holdings in foreign assets rules out a big exodus.
Also, economists say, the traditionally cautious pattern of French investment means there would be no swift move into equities and foreign markets.

Once French interest rates start rising, the flow out of money market funds that has supported the domestic bond market will start to dry up "as the French like to keep their money in money," one economist said. ($ = 5.788 French Francs)
